title: Chapter 114 — The Gilder
paragraphs: Pushing deeper and deeper into the heart of the Japanese cruising ground, the Pequod was soon in a constant bustle with the fishery. Often, in mild, pleasant weather, the crew spent twelve, fifteen, eighteen and twenty hours at a stretch in the boats, steadily rowing, sailing or paddling after the whales, or, for a spell of sixty or seventy minutes, waiting calmly for them to surface — though they had little success for all their trouble.

At such times, under a softened sun, afloat all day upon smooth, slow-heaving swells, seated in his boat as light as a birch canoe, and so sociably mingling with the soft waves themselves that, like hearthstone cats, they purr against the gunwale — these are the times of dreamy quietude, when beholding the tranquil beauty and brilliance of the ocean's skin, one forgets the tiger heart that pants beneath it; and would not willingly remember that this velvet paw but conceals a merciless fang.

At such times the wanderer in his whaleboat quietly feels a certain filial, trusting, land-like feeling toward the sea, and looks on it as so much flowery earth. The distant ship, with only the tops of her masts showing, seems to struggle forward not through high rolling waves but through the tall grass of a rolling prairie — the way the western emigrants' horses show only their pricked-up ears while their hidden bodies wade far and wide through the astonishing greenery.

The long-drawn virgin valleys; the mild blue hillsides; as the hush, the hum steals over these, you would almost swear that play-weary children lie sleeping in these solitudes, in some glad springtime, when the flowers of the woods are plucked. And all this mixes with your most mystic mood; so that fact and fancy, half-way meeting, interpenetrate and form one seamless whole.

Nor did such soothing scenes, however temporary, fail to have at least an equally temporary effect on Ahab. But if these secret golden keys did seem to open his own secret golden treasuries within him, his breath upon them proved only tarnishing.

Oh, grassy glades! Oh, endless landscapes of everlasting spring in the soul! In you — though you have long been parched by the dead drought of our earthy life — in you men can still roll like young horses in fresh morning clover, and for a few fleeting moments feel the cool dew of immortal life on them. I wish to God these blessed calms would last. But the mingled and mingling threads of life are woven warp and woof: calms crossed by storms, a storm for every calm. There is no steady progress in this life that never doubles back; we do not climb through fixed stages and then rest at the last one. We pass through infancy's unconscious spell, boyhood's unthinking faith, adolescence's doubt (the common fate), then skepticism, then disbelief, and come to rest at last in manhood's brooding repose of If. But once we have gone through it all, we go round the circle again, and are infants, boys and men, and Ifs, forever. Where is the final harbor, from which we will never cast off again? In what ecstatic ether does that world sail — the world that even the weariest will never tire of? Where is the foundling's father hidden? Our souls are like those orphans whose unmarried mothers die giving birth to them: the secret of who our father is lies in their grave, and we must go there to learn it.
That same day, too, Starbuck, gazing far down from the side of his boat into the same golden sea, murmured quietly:

"Loveliness unfathomable, as ever lover saw in his young bride's eye! Do not tell me of your teeth-tiered sharks and your kidnapping cannibal ways. Let faith oust fact; let fancy oust memory; I look deep down and do believe."
And Stubb, fish-like, with sparkling scales, leaped up in that same golden light:
"I'm Stubb, and Stubb has a history; but right here Stubb swears that he has always been jolly!"
